newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banks slow to pass on rate cuts - Buba.
newsitem.headline: German banks slow to pass on rate cuts - Buba.

text.p: German banks have become more hesitant in passing on cuts in official interest rates to borrowers, particularly small borrowers, in recent years, the Bundesbank said on Thursday.

Small borrowers are less likely to benefit from Bundesbank rate cuts than large debtors possibly because they are less able to find alternative means of financing, the Bundesbank said in its October monthly report.

"In the last rate cut cycle, which started in 1992, interest rates on overdrafts reacted particularly hesitantly to the fall in central bank rates in comparison with similar earlier periods," the Bundesbank said.
This is particularly true of "small" loans under one million marks, the Bundesbank said.
The gap between three-month money market rates and the rate on three-month bank loans widened to its current level of seven percentage points from about three in 1990.

The increasing gap was explained by a rising number of insolvencies during the period which boosted banks' risk provisioning costs, and by a rise in the cost of refinancing for banks, the report said.
By contrast, Bundesbank rate moves have a stronger impact on the interest rates banks pay on sight deposits, it said.
In fact, the gap between money market rates -- which are directly influenced by Bundesbank policy -- and deposit rates has narrowed in the 1990s, the Bundesbank said.
In addition, banks are becoming quicker at passing rate changes on into deposit rates, particularly for small investors, the report said.

"Increasingly, smaller customers are in a position to obtain market-conform terms whereas previously this tended only to be possible for large investors who had access to the Euromarket ...," the Bundesbank said.
That was partly because banks have been forced to offer higher interest rates on deposits to avoid losing customers to money market funds, which were introduced in Germany in 1994, the report said.

Successive reductions in the minimum reserve requirement -- the percentage of deposits banks must hold in non-interest bearing accounts at the Bundesbank -- have also helped narrow the gap between money market and deposit rates.
With the reserve requirement at two percent for sight deposits and money market rates currently at three percent, the requirement only justifies a gap of six basis points, the report said.
